articles.title: How I made quality non-negotiable in an Expo app
articles.excerpt: React Native apps don't usually fail loudly. They rot quietly. A refactor leaves a screen that return null and ships a blank page. A "temporary" stub passes lint, type-check, and unit tests because no…
articles.body: React Native apps don't usually fail loudly. They rot quietly. A refactor leaves a screen that return null and ships a blank page. A "temporary" stub passes lint, type-check, and unit tests because nothing renders it. A business rule everyone agreed on — "the wallet changes when you spend" — is never actually asserted, so it silently breaks three releases later. Tests don't catch these because tests check logic , and these are integration truths. So I made them impossible to skip, with two build gates that fail npm run check and CI. Gate 1 — a "screens gate": a screen must actually be a screen A stub screen (returns null , or renders nothing) is invisible to logic tests.

articles.title: A reader picked apart my benchmark. Here is what survived, and what changed
articles.excerpt: Last week I published a study of 181 real code changes, and one sentence in it was wrong. A reader found it by re-adding my numbers. This is what they found, what I changed, and what is still open. I'…
articles.body: Last week I published a study of 181 real code changes, and one sentence in it was wrong. A reader found it by re-adding my numbers. This is what they found, what I changed, and what is still open. The sentence I'd written that in 10% of agent-written pull requests every test failed on the old code only because the test file imports a name the change adds (so the file can't even load), and that "no maintainer commit in my sample looked like that." The reader re-derived my results files before reading the write-up. Every sum held. Then they pointed at a line I'd skipped: the maintainer file lists 9 tests with the verdict WEAK out of 212 (4%), while the agent file lists 79 out of 591 (13%). So the pattern isn't absent on the maintainer side. I went and looked.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.

articles.title: Four years ago, NASA punched an asteroid. Europe's Hera probe arrives this month to inspect the wreckage
articles.excerpt: NASA's DART mission made a cosmic mess four years ago — and now a new spacecraft is ready to scout out exactly what the first-of-its-kind collision accomplished.
articles.body: NASA's DART mission made a cosmic mess four years ago — and now a new spacecraft is ready to scout out exactly what the first-of-its-kind collision accomplished. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft slammed into a small space rock called Dimorphos on Sept. 26, 2022, in humanity's first test of planetary defense. That's the field dedicated to protecting Earth from the possibility of a calamitous asteroid impact, and DART mimicked how humans could change the orbit of a threatening space rock, taking it off its collision course. The mission definitely succeeded, shortening the little asteroid's orbit around a larger rock called Didymos by about 33 minutes .
